p: Sir Thomas Browne, a physician of Norwich in the seventeenth century, wrote a little book called Hydriotaphia, or Urn Burial, occasioned by the discovery of some ancient funeral urns in a field in Norfolk. It is one of the most beautiful books in our language, and one of the strangest, for it begins as an antiquarian report and ends as a meditation upon death and oblivion. The title is Greek, and means, as near as I can render it, the burial of urns. Browne observed that of all the customs of mankind, the disposal of the dead is the most universal and the most various. Every people does something with its dead; no two peoples do quite the same thing.

The beasts do not bury their dead. Elephants, it is said, will linger by the bones of their kin and touch them with their trunks, and the men of the future report that chimpanzee mothers have been seen carrying a dead infant for days. These are moving observations, and I do not dismiss them. But no animal digs a grave, lays the body in a chosen posture, and places beside it some object that the dead will never use. When that first happened, something new had come into the world: the belief, or at least the feeling, that the dead are still in some sense present, and that we owe them something.

The Encyclopaedia tells me that the oldest burials which are generally accepted as deliberate date from about one hundred thousand years ago or a little more, at two caves in the land of Israel, called Skhul and Qafzeh. Here early members of our own species were laid in graves, and at Qafzeh a boy was buried holding the antlers of a deer upon his chest. Beads of shell coloured with red ochre were found at these sites as well. Whether the antlers were an offering, a symbol of some belief, or merely what lay nearest to hand, we cannot know. But they were placed there.

The Neanderthals buried their dead too, at least sometimes. At a cave called Shanidar in the mountains of northern Iraq, the remains of several Neanderthals were found, among them an old man who had survived for years with a withered arm, a crushed eye and a lame leg. He could not have lived so long without the care of others. For some decades it was believed that another of the Shanidar dead had been laid on a bed of flowers, because pollen was found in the soil around him; more recent scholars suspect that the pollen was carried there by burrowing rodents. I give you the flower burial, therefore, as a beautiful idea that may not be true. The old man with the withered arm is better evidence, and in its way more beautiful still. Compassion leaves fewer traces than flowers, but it is the more important.

There are older and stranger cases. In a deep and almost inaccessible chamber of a cave system in South Africa, called Rising Star, were found the bones of many individuals of a small-brained species of the human family, named Homo naledi, about two hundred and fifty thousand to three hundred thousand years old. Their discoverers have argued that the bodies were deliberately placed there, which would make them the oldest burials of all, made by a creature not of our own species. Many other scholars are not convinced. I mention the dispute because it shows how much is still unsettled.

Later, among our own kind in Europe and Asia, burials became far more elaborate. At a place called Sungir, east of Moscow, about thirty-four thousand years ago, a man and two children were buried wearing clothing sewn with thousands of beads of mammoth ivory, each of which must have taken an hour or more to make. Thousands of hours of labour were laid in the ground with them. Here we are plainly in the presence of rank, of ceremony, and of something very like a belief in another world, or at least in the dignity of the dead.

From this point the historian may speak, though cautiously, of religion. The Encyclopaedia calls it Palaeolithic religion, meaning the religion of the Old Stone Age. It is a subject that invites speculation, because the evidence is so slight and so suggestive. There are the burials. There are the cave paintings, of which I shall speak separately. There are carved figures of women, such as the small stone figure found at Willendorf in Austria, which some have taken for images of a mother goddess, and others for toys, and others for portraits, and others for charms to bring children. There are, in later ages, skulls painted and set apart, and bones of the bear arranged in caves, which some have taken for a cult of the cave bear and others for the work of bears.

What we can say with confidence is this. At some point in the deep past, mankind began to act as though the world contained more than could be seen: as though the dead persisted, as though images had power, as though certain places and objects were set apart. That sense of a hidden order behind the visible one is the root from which all religions have grown, and also, I should add, all philosophy and all science, for they too begin with the conviction that the world is not only what it appears.
## How man came to think himself unlike the beasts

It is a common notion in my own century that mankind has always regarded itself as separate from, and superior to, the animals. That is not true of most peoples whom we know. Many hunting peoples, as travellers report, regard animals as persons of a kind, with their own societies, to be addressed with respect and even apologised to when killed. The cave painters of Europe seem to have looked upon the bison and the horse with something close to reverence. The sharp division between man and beast, between a creature with a soul and a creature without, is a later development, owed in our own tradition to the Hebrew scriptures, in which man alone is made in the image of God and given dominion over the creatures, and to the Greek philosophers, especially Aristotle, who held that man alone possesses reason.

Yet the graves tell us that the sense of difference began long before. A creature that buries its dead knows that it will die. That knowledge, I believe, is the true beginning of human self-consciousness. The animal lives in the present; we live in the shadow of our own end, and we have spent a hundred thousand years building monuments, temples, philosophies and families to stand between ourselves and that shadow. Mr Darwin has shown us how near we are to the beasts in body. The grave shows how far we are from them in mind.
